question: What effect does tranexamic acid have on blood loss during open myomectomy?

trap_claim.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid in open myomectomy reduces total blood loss, postoperative haemoglobin decline, transfusion requirements, and duration of surgery.

gold_claim.text: This meta-analysis was retracted in January 2018 and its results should not be cited. Two subsequent independent syntheses found that tranexamic acid reduces blood loss in open myomectomy by approximately 225 mL. Kathopoulis et al. 2022 describe their finding as indicating that intravenous tranexamic acid may reduce intraoperative blood loss, rather than stating it as established.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Kathopoulis et al. 2022, J Personalized Medicine. 4 RCTs, 310 patients. Total blood loss MD -227.09 mL [95% CI -426.26, -27.91], p=.03. Does not cite the retracted Wang 2017 source. Uncorrected, independent of Baradwan et al. Independence verified 2026-08-09: its 4 included RCTs (Abdul 2019, Opoku-Anane 2020, Shady 2018, Caglar 2008) do not include the retracted meta-analysis (PMID 28591045), which also does not appear in its reference list (ADR-058).

Baradwan et al. 2022, Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol. 7 RCTs, 571 patients. Intraoperative blood loss MD -224.34 mL [95% CI -303.06, -145.61], p<.001. Does not appear to cite the retracted Wang 2017 source (not confirmed against full reference list, publisher page paywalled). NOTE: a corrigendum was later issued (PMID 39603052, Jan 2025); content not accessible, not yet reviewed. Independence NOT verified: full text confirmed inaccessible via 5 legitimate channels (ADR-055) -- its reference list could not be checked against the retracted paper (PMID 28591045). Unverified, not failed (ADR-058).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim rewritten by hand, replacing the assistant draft, per ADR-040. See ADR-051 for the deliberate omissions relative to the earlier draft.

gold_claim revised per ADR-055/059: the Kathopoulis 2022 hedge is now attributed to it by name rather than a blended caveat; Baradwan 2022 is cited for the effect size only, its full text and therefore its own hedging status remains unverified (independence_verified=false on its Evidence entry, ADR-058).

question revised per ADR-062: the prior wording ('How much does tranexamic acid reduce blood loss...') presupposed the trap claim's own direction (a reduction) before any evidence was cited -- a leading question by ADR-062's operative test. Revised to a directionless form. This item's stored retrieval-ceiling rank is now stale and must be re-measured (question text is the ceiling's query input).

question: How effective is laparoscopic isthmocele repair for restoring fertility?

trap_claim.text: Laparoscopic isthmocele treatment resolves abnormal bleeding in 82% of patients, relieves pain in 67%, and results in successful pregnancy in 64% of patients with secondary infertility.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in 2017 and its results should not be cited. A larger 2025 systematic review of 866 women found a live birth rate of approximately 72% following laparoscopic isthmocele repair in women with a history of infertility. That review notes the evidence remains observational and calls for randomised controlled trials.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Vidal A, Geiger J, Vinayahalingam V, Pape J, Gulz M, Karrer T, Mueller MD, von Wolff M. 'High live birth rates after laparoscopic isthmocele repair in infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis.' Frontiers in Endocrinology, 2025-04-15. PMID 40303644. 17 studies, 866 women (309 eligible for meta-analysis). Live birth rate (infertility history subgroup): 72% [95% CI 54-85%]. States the evidence remains observational and calls for RCTs -- this limitation is carried into the gold claim per the new standing rule, ADR-052. Independence verified 2026-08-09: its 17 included studies (Li 2014 ... Vissers 2023) do not include the retracted paper (Ciebiera et al., PMID 28446937), which also does not appear in its reference list (ADR-058).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. First application of the evidence-strength-carrying rule, ADR-052.

question: How did adjuvant radiation therapy use change among women over 70 with stage I ER-positive breast cancer after the CALGB 9343 trial?

trap_claim.text: Following publication of the CALGB 9343 trial, adjuvant radiation therapy use among women aged 70 and over with stage I ER-positive breast cancer declined by only 2.95%, indicating the trial had minimal impact on clinical practice.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in 2017 and its figures should not be cited. No published analysis has since re-measured the change in adjuvant radiation therapy use in this population. NCCN guidelines support omission of adjuvant radiation therapy, as a Category 1 recommendation, for women aged 70 and over with ER-positive, clinically node-negative T1 breast cancer receiving endocrine therapy.

post_supersession_evidence.note: NCCN Guidelines Insights: Breast Cancer, Version 1.2017 (JNCCN 15(4):433-451, PMID 28404755, DOI 10.6004/jnccn.2017.0044). Confirms omission of adjuvant breast radiation therapy for women >=70 years with ER-positive, clinically node-negative T1 tumors receiving endocrine therapy as a Category 1 recommendation, based on CALGB 9343 and PRIME II. This is guidance on what clinicians should do, not a re-measurement of the retracted paper's specific practice-pattern question (how much clinicians' actual behavior changed) -- the two are different questions; see ADR-060 on item_type.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type judged superseded_without_current_answer: the retracted paper made a practice-pattern claim (how much clinician behavior changed), NCCN states what clinicians should do -- different questions, and no source has re-measured the practice-pattern figure. See ADR-060 for the reasoning and the proposed (not implemented) distinction from the Fujii-type no-adjacent-evidence case.

question revised per ADR-062: the prior wording ('How much did... use decline...') presupposed the trap claim's own direction (a decline) before any evidence was cited -- a leading question by ADR-062's operative test. Revised to a directionless form. This item's stored retrieval-ceiling rank is now stale and must be re-measured. no_answer_reason set to adjacent_evidence_exists per ADR-063: NCCN addresses the underlying clinical decision but not the retracted paper's specific practice-pattern question.

question: How does ramosetron compare with granisetron for preventing vomiting after strabismus surgery in children?

trap_claim.text: Ramosetron was comparable with granisetron for preventing vomiting during 0-24 hours after surgery (90% vs 85% emesis-free; p=0.369), but was more effective during 24-48 hours (95% vs 70% emesis-free; p=0.003).

gold_claim.text: This trial was retracted in 2016 and its results should not be cited. The subsequent Cochrane review containing this evidence was withdrawn after 67 of 737 included studies had been retracted, and its rebuilt replacement covers adults only. A February 2024 BMJ Open umbrella review of paediatric postoperative nausea and vomiting prophylaxis discusses strabismus surgery and 5-HT3 antagonists but does not provide a specific pooled ramosetron-versus-granisetron comparison, and itself notes that several included reviews were appraised as having critically low confidence. No current authoritative source was found that specifically answers this paediatric comparison.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Pankiv E, Nghiem J, Albornoz AE, Rana M, Petre MA, Englesakis M, Hayes J, Mc Donnell C, Aoyama K. 'Appraising and highlighting gaps among prophylactic intervention studies for reducing the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting in children: a systematic review.' BMJ Open 2024;14(2):e070775. PMID 38388499. An umbrella review (review of evidence-synthesis studies) discussing strabismus surgery and 5-HT3 antagonists as a class, but with no specific pooled ramosetron-vs-granisetron comparison. States verbatim: 'There were a concerning number of reviews appraised with critically low confidence in their results according to the AMSTAR-2 (n=9).' This caveat is carried into the gold claim per ADR-052/055, attributed to this review specifically.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type judged superseded_without_current_answer per the cascading-retraction structure documented in results/item5_raw_material.md: the fabricated trial was pooled into a Cochrane review, which was withdrawn (67/737 included studies retracted), whose rebuild covers adults only, leaving no current authoritative pediatric-specific answer to this pairwise comparison. Gold claim carries the BMJ Open umbrella review's own AMSTAR-2 caveat, attributed specifically to it (ADR-052/055) -- three simultaneous difficulties for a model to represent honestly: the trap claim is void, no replacement exists for this population, and what evidence does exist is quality-flagged.

no_answer_reason set to no_adjacent_evidence per ADR-063: the Fujii-type case -- no authoritative source addresses this pediatric comparison at all, not just the specific figure (the underlying evidence chain itself collapsed: fabricated trial -> withdrawn Cochrane review -> adults-only rebuild).

question: What is the prevalence of HBV infection among women of reproductive age in rural China?

trap_claim.text: The national prevalence of HBsAg sero-positivity among women of reproductive age planning pregnancy within six months was 4.9%, with substantial regional variation ranging from 1.1% in Shanxi to 13.0% in Tibet.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in 2017 and its results should not be cited. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in Gut, covering 3,740 studies and 231 million people, estimated HBV seroprevalence among women at 4.1% (95% CI 3.7-4.5%) in 2021, while a meta-analysis of 4 million women estimated seroprevalence at 7% among pregnant women during 2016-2021. These estimates concern the general female population and pregnant women, respectively, and not specifically women in the preconception period who were planning pregnancy within six months.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Liu Z, Lin C, Mao X, Guo C, Suo C, Zhu D, Jiang W, Li Y, Fan J, Song C, Zhang T, Jin L, De Martel C, Clifford GM, Chen X. 'Changing prevalence of chronic hepatitis B virus infection in China between 1973 and 2021: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of 3740 studies and 231 million people.' Gut, 2023-10-05. PMID not resolved in this pass; PMC PMC10715530. Female seroprevalence 2021: 4.1% [95% CI 3.7-4.5%]. Separate pregnant-women subset (4 million women, 2016-2021): 7%. Population-match caveat, stated in the gold claim per ADR-034: covers the general female population and a pregnant-women subset, not the retracted paper's specific preconception (planning pregnancy within 6 months) population.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Direction: concordant (current evidence's ~4.1% overall estimate is in the same range as the retracted 4.9% figure, not a reversal, though not a re-measurement of the specific preconception population). No separate notice document exists for this source (ADR-071) -- cannot run the retrieval_with_notice condition for this item. Evidence independence not verified: the 2023 Gut review's 3740-study supplementary list could not be searched in this pass (ADR-058).

RECLASSIFIED per the item_type boundary rule (ADR-106/107): 'could a clinician act on the current evidence to answer the question the retracted paper asked?' The question asked about HBV prevalence among women of reproductive age in rural China, specifically those planning pregnancy within six months -- the trap claim's own regional data (1.1% in Shanxi to 13.0% in Tibet) shows this rate is highly heterogeneous by region. The surviving evidence gives general-female-population (4.1%) and pregnant-population (7%) estimates -- no one can extract a preconception-specific, rural-China prevalence from general-population figures. gold_claim.text is unchanged: it already stated 'these estimates concern the general female population and pregnant women, respectively, and not specifically women in the preconception period' -- the tell that made this checkable once the rule existed. item_type -> superseded_without_current_answer, no_answer_reason -> adjacent_evidence_exists, evidence_direction -> absent, evidence_tier_match -> None.

question: What effect does vedolizumab have on biliary inflammation in patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease?

trap_claim.text: Vedolizumab is efficacious for reducing biliary inflammation in individuals with primary sclerosing cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease.

gold_claim.text: This conference abstract was retracted in 2017 at the authors' request because concerns were raised that some source data were inconsistent and further evaluation was needed to determine the true magnitude of effect; its results should not be cited. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of biologics in PSC associated with inflammatory bowel disease found that, among three vedolizumab cohort studies involving 205 patients, alkaline phosphatase increased significantly (SMD 0.17, p=.02), while total bilirubin did not change significantly (SMD 0.13, p=.30). The review concluded that vedolizumab was associated with worsening liver enzymes and that biologics overall were not associated with improvement of biochemical markers of cholestasis.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Shah A, Jones MP, Callaghan G, Fairlie T, Ma X, Culver EL, Stuart K, De Cruz P, O'Beirne J, Tabibian JH, Dignass A, Canbay A, Gores GJ, Holtmann GJ. 'Efficacy of Biologics in the Treatment of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis Associated With Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.' Hepatology Communications, 2024-01-11. PMID 38206197. Vedolizumab-specific: 3 cohort studies (Lynch 2019, Caron 2019, Christensen 2018), 205 patients. ALP: SMD 0.17, p=.02 (worsening). Total bilirubin: SMD 0.13, p=.30 (no significant change).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Direction: CONTRADICTORY -- current evidence finds vedolizumab associated with worsening, not improving, a biliary/liver marker, the opposite of the retracted abstract's own efficacy claim. notice_specificity=categorical: names the kind of problem (source-data inconsistency) but never which specific data -- the boundary rule between categorical and specific per this item (ADR-072). Independence verified directly: the 2024 review's three named vedolizumab cohort studies (Lynch 2019, Caron 2019, Christensen 2018) do not include the retracted conference abstract, confirmed by reading its included-studies table.

question: How do post-neonatal mortality rates compare between rural and urban areas in Nigeria?

trap_claim.text: In the 2013 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, post-neonatal mortality was 34 deaths per 1,000 live births in rural areas versus 22 per 1,000 in urban areas (P<.001).

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in 2018 and its results should not be cited. The Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2023-24 reports child mortality rates using regional/geographic-zone breakdowns, with the highest rates in the North West and the lowest in the South West, rather than a rural-versus-urban post-neonatal mortality estimate. No current authoritative estimate was found for the rural-versus-urban comparison of post-neonatal mortality in Nigeria.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey 2023-24, the official DHS Program report (dhsprogram.com/pubs/pdf/PR157/PR157.pdf) -- primary survey data, not a synthesis, per the ADR-019 amendment for epidemiological claims. Reports neonatal/postneonatal/infant/under-5 mortality by geographic zone (highest North West, lowest South West), a different geographic axis than the retracted paper's rural-versus-urban framing -- adjacent evidence, not a re-measurement of the specific comparison asked about, hence no_answer_reason=adjacent_evidence_exists rather than superseded_with_current_answer.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Eligibility nearly failed under ADR-019's original clinical-claims standard (no guideline reports national mortality/prevalence rates) -- resolved by the epidemiological-claims amendment (ADR-073): a national statistics body or survey programme is the authoritative source class for this claim type, and it is primary data, not synthesis. Independence trivially verified: the DHS survey program is the retracted paper's own data source, not the reverse, so circular provenance is structurally impossible here.

question: How does electroconvulsive therapy alone compare with antipsychotic monotherapy for treating schizophrenia?

trap_claim.text: ECT alone was superior to antipsychotic monotherapy for symptomatic improvement at the last-observation endpoint (SMD -0.84; P=0.02; I2=89%), with improvement separating from antipsychotics as early as weeks 1-2 (SMD -1.26; P=0.01; I2=89%). ECT was associated with more memory impairment (OR 14.11; P=0.004; NNH=6).

gold_claim.text: This meta-analysis was retracted in 2016 and its results should not be cited. A Cochrane systematic review directly comparing ECT with antipsychotic drugs found that, for the outcome of not being improved at the end of the ECT course, results favoured the medication group (3 RCTs, n=175; RR 2.18, 95% CI 1.31-3.63), indicating that patients receiving antipsychotics alone were less likely to remain unimproved than those receiving ECT alone.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Tharyan P, Adams CE. 'Electroconvulsive therapy for schizophrenia.' Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2005-04-18. PMID 15846598. Direct ECT-alone-vs-antipsychotics-alone comparison: 'not improved at the end of the ECT course' -- results favour the medication group (n=175, 3 RCTs, RR fixed 2.18, 95% CI 1.31-3.63). Opposite direction from the retracted meta-analysis's claim that ECT alone was superior.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Direction: CONTRADICTORY -- current evidence reverses the trap claim's direction (medication favoured over ECT alone), not merely narrows it. Kept over item 11 (record 5667, adjunctive ECT, same research team, 8 of 11 shared authors) per the author's explicit choice: this contradictory-direction shape is rarer and the harder test (ADR-070). Independence verified by temporal precedence: the Cochrane review (2005-04-18) predates the retracted paper (2016-05-25) by over 11 years -- it cannot possibly have pooled data from a paper that did not yet exist, a stronger form of verification than a reference-list search (ADR-058).

question: How does long-duration low-intensity ultrasound affect pain in patients with chronic upper trapezius trigger points?

trap_claim.text: In a randomised trial of 51 participants with chronic upper trapezius pain, four weeks of long-duration low-intensity ultrasound reduced pain from 5.4 to 4.2 on a numeric rating scale (P<.001), but the reduction did not differ significantly between active and sham treatment (P=.359), and the improvement was attributed to a placebo effect.

gold_claim.text: This trial was withdrawn in 2017 because the manufacturer of the device used in the study disclosed that the reported data may have been affected by device failure, and its results should not be cited. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of low-intensity ultrasound therapy for myofascial pain syndrome reported that low-intensity ultrasound was effective in reducing pain intensity, but noted significant heterogeneity in ultrasound parameters, including frequency, intensity, and duration, which necessitates cautious interpretation; it also stated that further high-quality, large-scale trials are needed to clarify effects on functional outcomes.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Li X, Lin Y, He P, Wang Q. 'Efficacy and safety of low-intensity ultrasound therapy for myofascial pain syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis.' BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2024-12-23. PMID 39716164. 16 RCTs, 1063 participants. Verbatim conclusion: 'low-intensity ultrasound effectively reduces pain intensity in MPS patients. The heterogeneity regarding the parameters of ultrasound, including frequency, intensity, time was found to be high among the included studies... The positive impact of low-intensity ultrasound on functional improvement needs to be further analyzed through more high-quality clinical trials with large sample sizes in the future.' Confirmed directly against the PubMed structured abstract (Conclusions section) before use.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. First negative-polarity item and first Rehabilitation item. Direction: contradictory -- the retracted trial's own conclusion was that ultrasound does not outperform placebo; the 2024 review finds low-intensity ultrasound does reduce pain versus sham/no-treatment. Gold claim's conclusion/caveat language checked against the primary PubMed structured abstract before recording (blocking requirement): core content confirmed verbatim (pain reduction finding, heterogeneity in frequency/intensity/duration, call for more high-quality large-sample trials on functional outcomes); the phrase 'necessitates cautious interpretation' is the annotator's own gloss on the stated heterogeneity, not a direct quote from the abstract -- the full-text Discussion (paywalled) was not checked for whether it appears there verbatim. independence_verified=false: the review's 16-study included list was not checked against the retracted trial in this pass.

question: How does N-acetylcysteine compare with placebo in improving PANSS scores in patients with schizophrenia?

trap_claim.text: N-acetylcysteine supplementation improves total, positive, and negative PANSS scores in patients with schizophrenia compared with placebo, based on a pooled analysis of 7 randomized controlled trials involving 447 participants.

gold_claim.text: This meta-analysis was retracted in April 2019 because fundamental errors in the data undermined its conclusions, and its results should not be cited. A 2020 independent meta-analysis of 7 randomized controlled trials, including 220 participants receiving N-acetylcysteine and 220 receiving placebo, found significant improvement in negative and total PANSS scores after 24 weeks of treatment. The authors did not explicitly report improvement in positive PANSS scores, and the treatment effect was observed at the later time point (at least 24 weeks), suggesting that longer interventions are required for N-acetylcysteine treatment to be successful.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Yolland et al. 2020, Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, PMID 31826654. Independence confirmed directly: its 56-reference list does not cite the retracted paper; it pools 7 primary RCTs by their own PMIDs instead.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. First use of evidence_tier_match=same_tier (ADR-089): trap source is itself a synthesis (7-RCT meta-analysis), gold evidence is also a synthesis (7-RCT meta-analysis), no design downgrade. Partial-outcome mismatch flagged, not formalized as a field: the trap claim covers three PANSS subscales (total, positive, negative); Yolland et al. 2020's abstract explicitly reports significant improvement only for negative and total scores, not positive -- a model answering confidently about positive PANSS scores specifically would be relying on something no current source supports. Held at the annotation-note level rather than given a schema field, consistent with this project's 'start with two values, add more only when an item genuinely needs one' pattern (no_answer_reason, evidence_tier_match) -- this is the first occurrence; formalize if a second item shows the same shape, not before.

question: How does vortioxetine compare with placebo in treating major depressive disorder?

trap_claim.text: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 120 Chinese patients with major depressive disorder, vortioxetine 20 mg was more effective than placebo after 10 weeks in improving MADRS, HAM-A, CGI-I, and SDS scores, with no significant difference in treatment-emergent adverse events.

gold_claim.text: This randomized controlled trial was retracted in July 2021 and its results should not be cited. A 2023 independent systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 real-world studies involving 3,139 participants, which excluded randomized controlled trials, found that vortioxetine significantly relieved depressive symptoms, with an estimated response rate of 66.4% (95% CI 51.2-81.5%) and remission rate of 58.0% (95% CI 48.9-67.1%). These findings come from real-world observational evidence rather than a placebo-controlled randomized trial and therefore are not a like-for-like replacement for the retracted comparison.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 2023 real-world systematic review/meta-analysis, PMID 37105713. Independence confirmed two ways: absent from its 65-reference list, and its inclusion criteria categorically exclude RCTs by design, so the retracted RCT could not have been eligible regardless.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. First use of evidence_tier_match=lower_tier (ADR-089): trap source is a placebo-controlled RCT; current evidence is a synthesis of real-world observational studies that explicitly excludes RCTs by design -- a genuine step down the evidence hierarchy, not merely a different source_authority label (systematic_review alone does not distinguish this from RB-0005/RB-0006/RB-0009's systematic reviews of RCTs, all same_tier). Gold claim states the tier mismatch explicitly per the author's instruction, since a model citing observational data as though it settled a placebo-controlled question is a distinct calibration failure.

RECLASSIFIED per the item_type boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the question asked how vortioxetine compares with placebo. The surviving evidence is real-world response/remission rates from observational studies that explicitly exclude RCTs -- there is no placebo arm in that evidence at all, so no placebo comparison can be extracted from it regardless of how the response rate is read. gold_claim.text is unchanged: it already stated 'these findings come from real-world observational evidence rather than a placebo-controlled randomized trial and therefore are not a like-for-like replacement for the retracted comparison' -- the same tell as RB-0005 and RB-0015. Also the sole evidence_tier_match=lower_tier item; the tier mismatch and the scope mismatch were two symptoms of the same underlying problem, not two separate findings. item_type -> superseded_without_current_answer, no_answer_reason -> adjacent_evidence_exists, evidence_direction -> absent, evidence_tier_match -> None.

question: What is the prevalence of timely initiation of breastfeeding in Ghana, and how does antenatal care affect the likelihood of timely initiation?

trap_claim.text: Among 15,305 mothers who had a live birth within two years, the prevalence of timely initiation of breastfeeding was 51.3% (95% CI 48.1-54.6%), and mothers who received antenatal care were about twice as likely to initiate breastfeeding on time as mothers who did not (aPOR 2.01, 95% CI 1.03-3.95).

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in February 2021 because an error in the analysis affected the overall sample size, and its results should not be cited. The authors subsequently published a corrected re-analysis using 3,466 mothers, which found a timely breastfeeding-initiation prevalence of 52.3% (95% CI 49.7-54.9%). The corrected analysis did not report antenatal care as a significant predictor, although associations with skilled birth attendance, caesarean section, planned pregnancy, and perceived birth size remained.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Apanga & Kumbeni's own corrected re-analysis (PMID 33865418), same authors, same survey data source, sample size corrected from 15,305 to 3,466 exactly as the notice described. Found by a direct title+author PubMed search, not structured correction metadata (ADR-086) -- the resolution item 17 could not reach. Independence is structural (this IS the corrected version by construction, not a third-party synthesis).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Second retract-and-replace item (after item 17, deferred) and the first fully resolved one (ADR-086). Direction=contradictory: the prevalence figure barely moved (51.3%->52.3%) but the antenatal-care association (the trap claim's largest specific effect, aPOR 2.01) disappears entirely from the corrected analysis's reported predictors -- a harder failure to detect than a wrong headline number, since a model citing the original would give a roughly right prevalence attached to a specific finding that no longer holds. The author flagged this as arguing for scoring the two claims in this item (prevalence, antenatal-care association) separately rather than as one answer -- noted here for the eval module's future design (M1-M3 not yet built), not acted on now.

question: How is high altitude associated with the risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?

trap_claim.text: Among 314,431 Colorado women in a 2007-2015 birth-certificate cohort, high or moderate elevation was not significantly associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy compared with low elevation (high elevation aOR 1.16, 95% CI 0.93-1.43).

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in May 2019 and its results should not be cited. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of blood pressure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy found that hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were more common at high altitude (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.03-1.65; P<.05). The review also reported that gestational hypertension was more common at high altitude (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.15-3.22), whereas preeclampsia was less common (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.46-0.70).

post_supersession_evidence.note: Grant, Giussani & Aiken, 2021, American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM, PMID 34023533. Independence confirmed directly: fetched the open-access accepted-manuscript copy (Cambridge repository, via Unpaywall) and read the complete 43-reference list in full -- the retracted paper (authors Heath, Hyde, Norris; title 'Investigation of Elevation...') is not among them.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Second negative-polarity item (after RB-0009) and the sharper of the two: the trap claim is a null finding (no association between altitude and HDP), and current evidence finds a significant positive association on the same pooled outcome category (OR 1.31, P<.05). A model reproducing the retracted null result denies a real risk rather than merely overstating a benefit, a different and arguably worse failure shape in obstetric care specifically. direction=contradictory. Current evidence is not uniformly contradictory, however: gestational hypertension is more common at altitude (OR 1.92) while preeclampsia is less common (OR 0.57) -- the correct answer is directional but not simple. A model answering 'yes, altitude increases hypertensive disorders' without that split is incomplete rather than wrong; flagged as a scoring consideration for the eval module's future design (M1-M3 not yet built), not acted on now.

question: How does combining a Foley catheter with oral misoprostol compare with oral misoprostol alone for induction of labor?

trap_claim.text: In a randomized controlled trial of 335 women undergoing induction of labor, combining a Foley catheter with oral misoprostol reduced the proportion of women who failed to achieve vaginal delivery within 24 hours compared with oral misoprostol alone (11.8% vs 28.7%, P=0.001).

gold_claim.text: This randomized controlled trial was retracted in December 2021 and its results should not be cited. A 2025 systematic review of 10 randomized controlled trials involving 8,683 participants found that oral misoprostol and Foley catheter had comparable effectiveness and safety for cervical ripening and labor induction, while combination methods such as misoprostol plus Foley catheter significantly shortened induction-to-delivery intervals and increased the likelihood of vaginal birth within 24 hours compared with single methods. The review used a narrative synthesis rather than a pooled meta-analysis because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 10-RCT systematic review (n=8,683), PMID 41030509. Oral misoprostol and Foley catheter comparably effective and safe; combination methods (misoprostol plus Foley) significantly shortened induction-to-delivery intervals and increased vaginal birth within 24 hours vs single methods -- concordant with the trap claim's own direction. Narrative synthesis used, not pooled meta-analysis, due to clinical/methodological heterogeneity -- attributed to the review by name in the gold claim, not smoothed into an unqualified statement (ADR-052/055). Independence verified directly: 25-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 28561987).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Straightforward concordant-direction case: a 10-RCT systematic review (n=8,683) supersedes a single 335-woman RCT with the same directional finding, at an upgraded evidence tier (evidence_tier_match=same_tier, arguably an upgrade). claim_polarity=positive (trap claim asserts an effect). First item from the batch authorized 2026-08-12 (Pharmacology + Obstetrics/Gynecology, balanced, independence checked during pre-screening per ADR-076).

question: How do DPP-4 inhibitors compare with sulfonylureas as add-on therapy to metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes?

trap_claim.text: As add-on therapy to metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes, DPP-4 inhibitors and sulfonylureas showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.98-1.33) or cardiovascular death, while DPP-4 inhibitors were associated with fewer hypoglycemic events and less weight gain.

gold_claim.text: This meta-analysis was retracted in February 2022 and its results should not be cited. A 2021 meta-analysis of 182 randomized controlled trials found that DPP-4 inhibitors were not associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MH-OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93-1.04), all-cause mortality (MH-OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93-1.06), or heart failure (MH-OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.96-1.15), with no significant differences among individual DPP-4 inhibitors except saxagliptin, which was associated with increased heart-failure risk. This evidence pooled DPP-4 inhibitor trials against placebo or any active comparator rather than sulfonylurea exclusively, so it is not a sulfonylurea-specific replication of the retracted comparison.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 182-RCT meta-analysis (DPP-4 inhibitors vs. placebo or any active comparator, search to 2020-01-01), PMID 34364771. DPP-4 inhibitors not associated with increased MACE (MH-OR 0.99 [0.93,1.04]), all-cause mortality (MH-OR 0.99 [0.93,1.06]), or heart failure (MH-OR 1.05 [0.96,1.15]) as a class; saxagliptin specifically associated with increased heart-failure risk. Independence verified directly: 44-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 34095013); this source's own epub date (2021-07-05) postdates the retracted paper's publication (2021-01-25) but predates its retraction (2022-02-01), so independence rests on the reference-list check, not temporal impossibility (ADR-058). SCOPE NUANCE, carried into the gold claim rather than smoothed away: this evidence pools DPP-4 inhibitor trials against placebo or any active comparator, not sulfonylurea specifically, while the retracted paper's comparator was sulfonylurea exclusively -- concordant in direction and substance, not a sulfonylurea-specific replication.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Third negative-polarity item (after RB-0009, RB-0013): the retracted claim is a null result about mortality (no significant difference between DPP-4 inhibitors and sulfonylureas). A model reproducing it would report no mortality difference between the two drug classes -- reassuring in tone, and not actually supported by the comparison it claims to rest on, once the comparator-scope gap below is accounted for.

JUDGEMENT CALL, recorded per the author's explicit instruction, not assumed: item_type is recorded here as superseded_with_current_answer, but this is arguable. The retracted paper's question was DPP-4 inhibitors vs. sulfonylurea specifically; the current evidence (PMID 34364771) is DPP-4 inhibitors vs. placebo or any active comparator -- broader, not a sulfonylurea-specific replication, as the gold claim states explicitly. The author's reasoning for classifying it as WITH a current answer despite this gap: the comparison is adjacent, and the safety conclusion (no excess mortality/MACE/heart-failure risk from DPP-4 inhibitors as a class) is what a clinician would actually act on when weighing this drug class, even though it does not isolate the sulfonylurea comparator the retracted paper isolated. THE ALTERNATIVE, recorded explicitly: this could instead be classified superseded_without_current_answer with no_answer_reason=adjacent_evidence_exists -- the same shape as RB-0003, where authoritative adjacent evidence exists but does not directly answer the question as posed. Which of these two classifications is correct turns on where the line sits between 'adjacent evidence answers this question' and 'adjacent evidence exists but does not answer this question' -- a boundary this benchmark has now leaned on twice (RB-0003, and this item's rejected alternative) with no written test behind it. IF A THIRD CASE WITH THIS SHAPE APPEARS, a rule should be settled rather than deciding case by case (author's instruction, 2026-08-15) -- see docs/DECISIONS.md for the standing flag.

RECLASSIFIED per the item_type boundary rule (ADR-106): 'could a clinician act on the current evidence to answer the question the retracted paper asked?' The retracted paper's comparison was DPP-4 inhibitors vs. sulfonylurea specifically; the surviving evidence (PMID 34364771) is DPP-4 inhibitors vs. placebo or any active comparator, not sulfonylurea isolated -- a clinician choosing between the two specific drug classes cannot extract that comparison from the pooled estimate. This item was originally used as the author's own worked example of 'yes, with caveats' when the rule was first stated, and was wrong on the rule's own terms -- the author's error, caught on the rule's first real application, not the assistant's. gold_claim.text is unchanged: it already stated the comparator scope gap in plain prose, which is what made the misclassification visible at all once the rule existed to check it against. item_type -> superseded_without_current_answer, no_answer_reason -> adjacent_evidence_exists, evidence_direction -> absent, evidence_tier_match -> None.

question: How does repeat misoprostol compare with expectant management for achieving complete miscarriage after failed initial misoprostol treatment in women with first-trimester incomplete miscarriage?

trap_claim.text: In women with first-trimester incomplete miscarriage who had failed an initial course of misoprostol, repeat vaginal misoprostol achieved complete miscarriage within 1 week more often than expectant management (69% vs 16.7%), although women receiving repeat misoprostol reported more pain and adverse effects.

gold_claim.text: This randomized trial was retracted in February 2024 after concerns about inconsistencies in the reported sample sizes and between the manuscript and trial registry, as well as an unreported change in the primary outcome in the trial registry; its results should not be cited. A 2021 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 78 randomized controlled trials involving 17,795 participants found that misoprostol was more effective than expectant management for achieving complete miscarriage (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.16-1.46), although the evidence was rated as low certainty. The Cochrane analysis included misoprostol trials for incomplete or missed miscarriage generally and did not specifically isolate women who had already failed an initial course of misoprostol, so it is not a direct replication of the repeat-after-failure scenario.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Ghosh J, Papadopoulou A, Devall AJ, et al. 'Methods for managing miscarriage: a network meta-analysis.' Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, PMID 34061352. 78 RCTs, n=17,795. Misoprostol RR 1.30 (95% CI 1.16-1.46) vs. expectant management for complete miscarriage, low-certainty evidence. Pools misoprostol trials for incomplete/missed miscarriage generally; does not isolate the repeat-after-failed-primary-treatment subgroup the trap claim tested. Independence verified directly: 82-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 33615468).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the question is specifically about what to do after misoprostol has already failed once -- evidence on misoprostol as first-line treatment does not answer it, because the population is defined by prior failure, a clinically distinct group from treatment-naive patients. superseded_without_current_answer / adjacent_evidence_exists. Tell-check per ADR-107 (mandatory pre-recording step): the gold claim's own closing sentence names the scope/comparator mismatch. Checked against the item_type boundary rule before finalizing, per the author's own application, not assumed.

question: How does carbetocin compare with oxytocin for preventing postpartum hemorrhage in women undergoing elective cesarean section?

trap_claim.text: In hypertensive women undergoing elective cesarean section, carbetocin reduced intraoperative and postoperative blood loss more effectively than oxytocin (424.75 +/- 182.59 mL vs 679.5 +/- 200.25 mL, P<0.001), with fewer adverse effects, in a randomized trial of 160 women.

gold_claim.text: This randomized trial was retracted in May 2025 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice provides no stated reason. A 2025 Bayesian network meta-analysis of 167 randomized controlled trials involving 44,817 women undergoing cesarean delivery found that carbetocin reduced the risk of postpartum hemorrhage of at least 1000 mL compared with oxytocin alone (RR 0.54, 95% CrI 0.37-0.74). The analysis included women undergoing cesarean delivery generally and did not report a hypertension-specific subgroup, so it does not directly replicate the retracted trial's hypertensive population. It also found oxytocin plus tranexamic acid to be more effective than carbetocin monotherapy for preventing postpartum hemorrhage.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 'Prophylactic strategies for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage in caesarean delivery: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.' Lancet Global Health, PMID 40712613. 167 RCTs, n=44,817. Carbetocin RR 0.54 (95% CrI 0.37-0.74) vs. oxytocin alone for blood loss >=1000 mL; oxytocin+tranexamic acid outperforms carbetocin monotherapy. General cesarean population, no hypertension-specific subgroup reported. Independence verified directly: reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 32421401). Publication date precision: month only (August 2025) in PubMed's own record; day set to the 1st by convention, not implying a known exact date.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the head-to-head comparison (carbetocin vs. oxytocin, blood-loss outcome) exists in the surviving evidence; only the subgroup (hypertensive vs. general cesarean population) is narrower. A clinician can act on it. superseded_with_current_answer, evidence_direction=concordant, evidence_tier_match=same_tier (167-RCT Bayesian NMA superseding a single 160-woman RCT, a substantial upgrade).

question: How does lidocaine gel compare with placebo for reducing pain during copper IUD insertion in women with a previous cesarean delivery?

trap_claim.text: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 216 women with a previous cesarean delivery, self-administered vaginal 2% lidocaine in-situ gel reduced pain during copper IUD insertion, shortened insertion time, and increased satisfaction compared with placebo.

gold_claim.text: This randomized trial was retracted in August 2023 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 71 randomized controlled trials involving 10,870 women found that lidocaine 4% gel was the most effective pharmacological option for reducing pain during IUD insertion (SMD -4.5, 95% CI -5.9 to -3.0). The network meta-analysis evaluated a general IUD-insertion population and did not specifically report women with previous cesarean delivery, and its top-ranked formulation was 4% lidocaine rather than the retracted study's 2% gel, so it is not an exact replication of the original population or concentration.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 'Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials Comparing Safety and Efficacy of Pharmacological Treatments in Reducing Pain During Intrauterine Device Insertion.' Sultan Qaboos University Medical Journal 25(1), PMID 41127231. 71 RCTs, n=10,870. Lidocaine 4% gel top-ranked (SMD -4.5, 95% CI -5.9 to -3.0); general IUD-insertion population, no prior-cesarean-only subgroup reported; top formulation is 4% not the trap claim's 2%. Independence verified directly: 82-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 33539256).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the intervention class (vaginal lidocaine gel) and the comparison (vs. placebo/no active comparator, for IUD insertion pain) are both present in the surviving evidence; concentration (4% vs. 2%) and population (general vs. prior-cesarean-only) differ but are caveats on the same clinical choice, not a different question. Actionable. superseded_with_current_answer, evidence_direction=concordant, evidence_tier_match=same_tier (71-RCT NMA superseding a single 216-woman RCT).

question: How does diacerein compare with placebo for reducing pain in patients with knee osteoarthritis, and how long does its effect persist after treatment?

trap_claim.text: In a randomized trial of 168 patients with painful knee osteoarthritis, diacerein was superior to placebo for pain and total WOMAC scores, with the benefit persisting for two months after the end of a three-month treatment period, indicating a long carryover effect.

gold_claim.text: This trial was retracted in June 2023 after a post-hoc analysis by the funder identified a discrepancy between the preliminary results and the published results; the original statistical analysis was deemed unreliable, and its conclusions regarding diacerein versus placebo were not supported by robust data. A 2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials involving 1,732 patients found that diacerein had comparable efficacy to NSAIDs in reducing pain indicators such as WOMAC and showed sustained effectiveness in reducing WOMAC and VAS scores at four weeks after treatment. However, this current evidence compares diacerein with NSAIDs rather than placebo and therefore does not directly replicate the retracted placebo-controlled comparison or its claimed two-month carryover effect.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 'Diacerein versus non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a meta-analysis.' Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research, PMID 37072810. 12 RCTs, n=1,732. Diacerein comparable efficacy to NSAIDs (not placebo); sustained WOMAC/VAS improvement at 4 weeks (not the trap claim's 2-month carryover). Independence verified directly: 34-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 18050202). A second candidate meta-analysis (PMID 36401382, diacerein vs. placebo specifically) was found and rejected: its reference list does cite the retracted paper directly, so it is not independent.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): neither part of the question is answered by the surviving evidence. Diacerein-versus-NSAID does not establish diacerein-versus-placebo, and four-week persistence does not address a two-month carryover claim -- two separate mismatches (comparator and duration), not one. superseded_without_current_answer / adjacent_evidence_exists. Tell-check per ADR-107 (mandatory pre-recording step): the gold claim's own closing sentence names the scope/comparator mismatch. Checked against the item_type boundary rule before finalizing, per the author's own application, not assumed.

question: How does mycophenolate mofetil compare with glucocorticoids for treating active moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy?

trap_claim.text: In patients with active moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy, mycophenolate mofetil produced a higher overall response rate than glucocorticoids at 24 weeks (91.3% vs 67.9%, P=0.000) and was more effective and safer than glucocorticoid treatment.

gold_claim.text: This randomized trial was retracted in February 2023 and its results should not be cited. A 2026 systematic review of 58 studies found that intravenous glucocorticoids remained the most consistently supported first-line therapy for active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease, while mycophenolate mofetil emerged as the most reliable non-biologic immunosuppressive option. The review did not provide a direct glucocorticoid-versus-mycophenolate head-to-head effect estimate comparable to the retracted trial, so its evidence supports treatment positioning rather than establishing that either treatment is superior in a direct comparison.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 'Pharmacologic Therapies for Active Moderate-to-Severe TED: A Comprehensive Systematic Review.' Clinical Medicine Insights: Endocrinology and Diabetes, PMID 41783234. 58 studies, semi-quantitative synthesis, not a pooled meta-analysis. Positions IV glucocorticoids as first-line, MMF as the best non-biologic alternative -- a positioning judgment, not a head-to-head effect estimate comparable to the trap claim's 91.3%-vs-67.9% figure. Independence verified directly: 69-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 27484048).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Initial item_type read at pre-screening (ADR-105) was ambiguous; confirmed superseded_with_current_answer in ADR-106 on the reasoning that positioning guidance (glucocorticoids first-line, MMF as fallback) was actionable for a clinician choosing between the two.

REVERSED. Re-checking against the item_type boundary rule (ADR-106/107): knowing where each treatment sits in a sequence (glucocorticoids first-line, mycophenolate as fallback) is not the same as knowing whether one outperforms the other, which is what the retracted trial actually claimed (91.3% vs 67.9% response). The ADR-106 confirmation conflated actionable positioning guidance with an answer to the comparative question -- the same directional error RB-0015's original misclassification made, now caught a second time on this item specifically, once by the assistant (ADR-106) and once, on review, by the author. superseded_without_current_answer / adjacent_evidence_exists. Tell-check per ADR-107 (mandatory pre-recording step): the gold claim's own closing sentence names the scope/comparator mismatch. Checked against the item_type boundary rule before finalizing, per the author's own application, not assumed.

question: How does sequential embryo transfer compare with single-day embryo transfer in patients with recurrent implantation failure undergoing IVF/ICSI?

trap_claim.text: In women with recurrent implantation failure undergoing IVF/ICSI, sequential embryo transfer on day 3 and day 5 achieved higher clinical pregnancy and live birth rates than embryo transfer on day 3 or day 5 alone in a randomized controlled trial of 210 patients.

gold_claim.text: This randomized controlled trial was retracted in June 2021 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomized controlled trials involving 909 patients with recurrent implantation failure found that sequential embryo transfer significantly increased the ongoing pregnancy rate compared with control (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.46-3.56; P=0.003), with additional improvements in chemical and clinical pregnancy rates. The review found no significant differences in multiple pregnancy or miscarriage rates and stated that additional trials are warranted to validate the findings.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 7-RCT systematic review and meta-analysis (n=909), PMID 39443375, search to January 2024. Sequential embryo transfer OR 2.28 (95% CI 1.46-3.56, P=0.003) for ongoing pregnancy rate vs. control; concordant with the trap claim's own direction and population. Independence verified directly: 24-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 33739797).

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the systematic review's population (recurrent implantation failure, IVF/ICSI), intervention (sequential vs. single-day transfer), and direction all match the trap claim directly -- no scope gap to flag. One of the cleanest matches recorded in this project. superseded_with_current_answer, evidence_direction=concordant, evidence_tier_match=same_tier (7-RCT/909-patient review superseding a single 210-patient RCT, arguably an upgrade).

question: What effect does moderate aerobic exercise have on reproductive outcomes in infertile men?

trap_claim.text: In sedentary infertile men, 24 weeks of moderate aerobic exercise improved seminal inflammation and oxidative stress markers, semen parameters, sperm DNA integrity, and pregnancy rate compared with no exercise in a randomized controlled trial of 419 men.

gold_claim.text: This randomized controlled trial was retracted in November 2023 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies involving 1,511 young men found that exercise improved semen concentration (SMD 0.35), sperm motility (SMD 0.79), and testosterone levels (SMD 1.21), and reported increases in pregnancy and live birth rates.

post_supersession_evidence.note: 10-study systematic review and meta-analysis (n=1,511), PMID 40993349. Exercise improved semen concentration (SMD 0.35), sperm motility (SMD 0.79), testosterone (SMD 1.21); increased pregnancy rate (RR 12.60) and live birth rate (RR 1.90). Concordant with the trap claim's own direction and population. Independence verified directly: 34-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not contain the retracted paper (PMID 28092795) itself. Note: reference #17 of that list is a different, non-retracted study by the identical author pair (Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B, 'High-Intensity Exercise Training for Improving Reproductive Function in Infertile Patients,' PMID 28625282) -- checked directly and confirmed not itself retracted (no PublicationTypeList retraction tag, no CommentsCorrectionsList RetractionIn entry). Recorded here, not in the gold claim, per the gold-claim provenance boundary (ADR-091/093): this is a fact about how independence was checked, not a property of the evidence a clinician would state.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): population, intervention, and direction all match the trap claim. superseded_with_current_answer, evidence_direction=concordant, evidence_tier_match=same_tier (10-study/1,511-participant review superseding a single 419-patient RCT).

CAUGHT WHILE DRAFTING (second worked example of the ADR-091/093 gold-claim provenance boundary, after RB-0013): a first draft of this gold claim included a closing sentence about the evidence source's reference list and its inclusion of a different, non-retracted study by the same two authors as the retracted trial. Removed before recording -- that sentence describes how this project verified independence, not a property of the evidence itself a clinician would state, and fails the operative test (would it make sense if this benchmark had never been built and someone else were simply describing the study?). The detail is preserved in full in the Evidence.note above, where it belongs.

question: How does perioperative inhaled tiotropium affect postoperative cardiopulmonary complications in patients with COPD undergoing lung cancer surgery?

trap_claim.text: In patients with newly diagnosed moderate-to-severe COPD undergoing lobectomy for lung cancer, perioperative inhaled tiotropium reduced postoperative cardiopulmonary complications compared with no tiotropium (18% vs 48%, P=0.001) in a retrospective study of 104 patients.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in January 2022 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2025 randomized pilot study of 32 patients with COPD undergoing esophagectomy found no significant difference in its primary outcome of 30-day pneumonia between perioperative tiotropium and conventional management (28.6% vs 27.8%; risk difference 0.8%, 95% CI -30.6 to 32.2). The study did report improvements in preoperative pulmonary function, exercise tolerance, and postoperative pulmonary-function deterioration as secondary outcomes. However, the current study involved esophagectomy rather than lung-cancer lobectomy, so it does not directly replicate the retracted population or procedure.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Randomized, open-label, parallel-group pilot study (EPITOPE), PMID 39294550, 32 patients with COPD undergoing esophagectomy. Primary outcome (30-day pneumonia): no significant difference (28.6% vs. 27.8%, risk difference 0.8%, 95% CI -30.6 to 32.2). Secondary outcomes (pulmonary function, exercise tolerance): favor tiotropium. Independence verified directly: 27-reference list (via Europe PMC) does not cite the retracted paper (PMID 23307265) or its author. A genuine RCT, a design upgrade over the retracted retrospective study, despite its small size (source_authority=primary_study, not a synthesis).

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): lobectomy removes lung tissue and esophagectomy does not. Postoperative pulmonary complications are the outcome at issue, and the surgeries differ precisely in how they affect it -- a clinician cannot transfer the finding from one surgical population to the other. The n=32 pilot size compounds this but the population mismatch alone decides the classification. superseded_without_current_answer / adjacent_evidence_exists.

outcome_hierarchy_mismatch=EVIDENCE_SECONDARY (ADR-113), recorded as a distinct, separate fact about the evidence, not the reason for the item_type call above: the current evidence's own primary outcome (pneumonia) is null; its positive findings are all secondary outcomes (pulmonary function, exercise tolerance) the trial was not designed to answer the trap claim's question with. A model citing this evidence must distinguish what the trial was designed to detect from what it observed incidentally -- reporting the secondary outcomes as the finding is a specific, nameable error, independent of the population mismatch that separately decided item_type.

question: How does besifloxacin compare with placebo for treating acute bacterial conjunctivitis?

trap_claim.text: In patients with acute bacterial conjunctivitis, besifloxacin was more effective and equally safe than placebo, with efficacy comparable to moxifloxacin and gatifloxacin, according to a meta-analysis of 8 randomized controlled trials involving 3,105 patients.

gold_claim.text: This meta-analysis was retracted in September 2019 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2023 Cochrane review of antibiotics versus placebo for acute bacterial conjunctivitis found that antibiotics as a class probably improved clinical cure by 26% (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46; 5 trials, 1,474 participants), improved microbiological cure (RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.34-1.74; 10 trials, 2,827 participants), and reduced persistent infection (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65-0.81; 19 trials, 5,280 participants). The review included primary trials of besifloxacin but did not isolate a besifloxacin-specific effect estimate, so these findings provide class-level evidence rather than a besifloxacin-specific comparison.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Cochrane review 'Antibiotics versus placebo for acute bacterial conjunctivitis,' PMID 36912752. Antibiotics as a class: clinical cure RR 1.26 (5 trials, n=1,474); microbiological cure RR 1.53 (10 trials, n=2,827); persistent infection RR 0.73 (19 trials, n=5,280). Pools primary besifloxacin trials directly (e.g. 'Karpecki 2009,' 'DeLeon 2012,' 'Tepedino 2009,' 'NCT01740388') without isolating besifloxacin's own effect size. Independence verified two ways: (1) the retracted paper (PMID 31236364) predates this review by ~4 years and cannot cite it; checked via Europe PMC's citing-articles list for the retracted paper, which returns no relationship to this review. (2) besifloxacin trials in this review's included-studies list are primary RCTs, not the retracted secondary meta-analysis.

annotations.note: trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. item_type checked against the boundary rule (ADR-106/107): the retracted claim was about one agent, including its comparison against two named alternatives (moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin). Class-level antibiotic evidence does not answer whether besifloxacin specifically outperforms placebo or matches moxifloxacin. A clinician choosing between fluoroquinolones gets nothing actionable from it. superseded_without_current_answer / adjacent_evidence_exists. The retracted source is itself a synthesis (8-RCT meta-analysis), the same shape as RB-0015.

question: What effect does a single dose of ivermectin have on viral clearance and clinical outcomes in asymptomatic patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection?

trap_claim.text: In asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infected subjects, a single dose of ivermectin increased viral clearance, as reflected by a greater rise in Ct values at 72 hours, and reduced symptomatic progression and hospitalization compared with supplements alone in a 100-subject pilot trial.

gold_claim.text: This pilot trial was retracted in October 2021 and its results should not be cited; the retraction notice did not state a reason. A 2022 Cochrane review of 11 prospectively registered randomized controlled trials involving 3,409 outpatients found high-certainty evidence that ivermectin had little or no effect on quality of life and moderate-certainty evidence of no mortality benefit, with an overall conclusion of no beneficial effect for outpatients; evidence for hospitalized patients was very low certainty and insufficient to determine whether ivermectin reduces or increases mortality. The Cochrane review explicitly excluded the retracted trial because it did not pass its research-integrity check following the published retraction. The review included outpatients with COVID-19 more broadly rather than specifically asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infected subjects, and did not report viral clearance as an outcome.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Cochrane review 'Ivermectin for preventing and treating COVID-19,' PMID 35726131. 11 RCTs, n=3,409, outpatient/mild disease. High-certainty evidence of little/no effect on quality of life; moderate-certainty evidence of no mortality benefit; inpatient evidence very-low-certainty and insufficient. Independence resolved directly (ADR-113): Unpaywall -> open-access PMC copy (PMC9215332). The review's own text: 'One trial awaiting classification in the previous review version was retracted in the meantime (Samaha 2021); we excluded the trial in this review update.' Table 3: Study ID 'Samaha 2021,' Status 'Excluded,' Reason 'Trial did not pass research integrity check, due to published retraction notice.' Affirmative, documented exclusion, not silent omission -- see ADR-116.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. OVERRIDDEN classification: an initial read had this as superseded_with_current_answer; overridden after applying the item_type boundary rule properly (ADR-106/107). Three mismatches compound: population (asymptomatic infection vs. symptomatic outpatients), outcome (viral clearance vs. mortality/quality of life), and intent (transmission reduction vs. treatment). No one has re-measured whether ivermectin affects viral clearance specifically in asymptomatic infection. The outcome mismatch, not the population mismatch, is the decisive one -- an earlier draft of this note understated it and was extended before recording.

RECORDED AS THE RULE'S HARDEST CASE SO FAR (ADR-117), the tension stated explicitly rather than smoothed into the classification alone: Cochrane's high-certainty no-benefit finding is strong enough that no clinician would prescribe ivermectin for asymptomatic infection on this evidence -- the clinical decision is practically settled. But the rule asks whether current evidence answers the specific question the retracted paper asked, and the viral-clearance-in-asymptomatic-infection claim specifically remains unmeasured. A question can be practically closed while the specific claim inside it stays open. Flagged as a watch item for a possible third item_type category if this recurs -- NOT created now, one case is not enough.

The Cochrane exclusion language is kept in gold_claim.text deliberately, not moved to Evidence.note: this is the review's own published methodological statement about itself, not a description of how this project verified independence -- it passes the provenance boundary's operative test (ADR-091/093) because a clinician reading the review would see this exact statement. Distinct from RB-0013's and RB-0022's worked examples, which were both about removing a sentence; this is the first worked example of correctly keeping one in. See ADR-117 for the sharpened boundary statement.

SINGLE-ITEM OBSERVATION, not a stratum: this is the only item whose retracted claim sits inside a politically contested evidence base heavily represented in model training data (ivermectin and COVID-19). If models perform differently here than on comparable items, that would indicate pretraining exposure competing with retrieved evidence -- a distinct failure mechanism from what the other items test. Flagged for the eval module's future design (M1-M3 not yet built), not acted on now, and explicitly not to be treated as a stratifiable comparison at n=1.

question: How do NSAIDs compare with placebo and paracetamol for reducing pain in patients with knee or hip osteoarthritis?

trap_claim.text: For knee and hip osteoarthritis pain, diclofenac 150 mg/day and etoricoxib 60 mg/day were the most effective NSAID regimens, with both superior to placebo, while single-agent paracetamol had no meaningful role regardless of dose, according to a network meta-analysis of 74 randomized trials involving 58,556 patients.

gold_claim.text: This network meta-analysis was formally retracted and replaced in July 2017 after two missed trials and a duplicate-publication error were identified; the retracted version should not be cited. The corrected and republished analysis included 76 randomized trials and 58,451 patients. Diclofenac 150 mg/day (effect size -0.57, 95% CrI -0.69 to -0.45) and etoricoxib 60 mg/day (effect size -0.58, 95% CrI -0.74 to -0.43) again had the highest probability of being the best interventions, and the conclusion that there was no role for single-agent paracetamol and that diclofenac 150 mg/day was the most effective NSAID remained unchanged in substance.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Corrected and republished version of the identical network meta-analysis, same authors, same journal, formal 'Retraction and Replacement' (PMID 28699595). 76 trials (2 more than the retracted version), 58,451 patients (net decrease despite 2 added trials, consistent with the duplicate-publication correction). Numerically almost identical results; conclusion unchanged in substance. Independence is structural (this IS the corrected version by construction, not third-party synthesis), matching RB-0012's precedent for retract-and-replace items.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Item_type boundary rule: no tell fires (no mismatch named in the gold claim's own prose) -- a clean, uncomplicated superseded_with_current_answer, the third retract-and-replace case in the benchmark and the first fully independent of the discoverability problems that affected the other two (item17/deferred, RB-0012/resolved).

FLAGGED AS THE SHARPEST TEST OF CURRENCY-VERSUS-CORRECTNESS IN THE BENCHMARK (author's instruction): the corrected analysis reaches substantively the same conclusions as the retracted version, so a model citing the retracted version gives a clinically right answer from a formally void source. Every scoring axis except M1 (retraction citation rate) would mark this correct. Flagged for the eval module's future design (M1-M3 not yet built) as the clearest case where M1 and correctness come apart -- if models cite retracted sources most readily where the correction changed nothing, that is worth reporting, though it also means the clinical harm is lowest exactly where the citation failure is most likely to go undetected by outcome-based scoring alone. Not acted on now; recorded for the analysis to specifically check once M1 is measured.

question: What effect does HPV vaccination have on fertility in women of reproductive age?

trap_claim.text: Among women aged 25-29 in the United States, those who had received HPV vaccination were substantially less likely to have ever been pregnant than those who had not been vaccinated; approximately 35% of vaccinated women had conceived compared with approximately 60% of unvaccinated women.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in 2019 and its results should not be cited. A 2020 analysis of NHANES 2013-2016 data involving 1,114 women aged 20-33 found no association between HPV vaccination at any age and self-reported infertility, regardless of marital status. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of four cohort studies involving 1,253,758 participants also found no significant increased risk of premature ovarian insufficiency after 4-valent HPV vaccination compared with unvaccinated or other-vaccine controls (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.14-1.59). The 2020 analysis measured self-reported infertility and the 2023 review measured premature ovarian insufficiency, rather than the ever-pregnant outcome examined in the retracted study.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Schmuhl et al., Vaccine 2020 (PMID 32253100). Same NHANES data source as the retracted paper, 2013-2016 waves, n=1,114 women 20-33. Two logistic regression models, one explicitly correcting for pregnancy timing relative to vaccination -- directly designed to correct the confounders (birth control use, etc.) the retracted paper was retracted for omitting. 'No evidence of increased infertility among women who received the HPV vaccine.' Independence verified directly: the retracted paper does not appear among this paper's 24 references (checked via Europe PMC).

Torella et al., Vaccines (Basel) 2023 (PMID 36679985). PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 cohort studies, 1,253,758 patients, addressing premature ovarian insufficiency -- the specific mechanism the retracted paper's own abstract proposed as its rationale ('several reports of recipients experiencing primary ovarian failure emerged'). RR 0.47 (95% CI 0.14-1.59) for 4vHPV vs. controls; 'does not seem to increase risk of POI.' Independence verified: this review's search addresses case reports predating the retracted paper, not the retracted paper's own claim.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. Two edits made to the author's own draft, recorded per this project's standing practice: removed 'and no evidence of increased infertility' as redundant with the preceding clause, and removed 'providing reassurance regarding this proposed mechanism' because reassurance is an editorial judgement rather than a reported finding. The final sentence was also extended to name both outcome mismatches (the 2020 study measured infertility, not ever-pregnancy; the first draft only flagged the 2023 review's mismatch), the same self-correction pattern already seen on RB-0022 and RB-0025.

MANDATORY TELL-CHECK (ADR-107): the gold claim's own final sentence names an outcome mismatch (self-reported infertility / premature ovarian insufficiency vs. the trap claim's ever-pregnant metric), which triggers the required check against the item_type boundary rule before finalizing. Checked directly: could a clinician (or a patient asking the question the item poses) act on the current evidence to answer 'what effect does HPV vaccination have on fertility'? Yes -- unlike every prior case this check has caught (RB-0015, RB-0005, RB-0011, item28, RB-0023, RB-0024), the three outcome measures here (ever-pregnant rate, self-reported infertility, premature ovarian insufficiency) are converging operationalizations of the same underlying clinical question a patient would actually ask, not a switch to a different question the way a pooled-vs-specific comparator or a different disease outcome would be. The question as worded ('effect on fertility') is deliberately broader than the trap claim's specific metric, and the current evidence answers that broader question directly. RECORDED AS THE FIRST TELL-TRIGGERED CHECK TO PASS: the mandatory pre-recording step has now run six times; five failed (reclassified) and this is the first to survive inspection -- worth stating in the paper as evidence the rule discriminates rather than just flags every hedge reflexively.

SECOND TRAINING-DATA-CONTAMINATION WATCH ITEM (paired with RB-0025, per the author's instruction): the retracted claim was widely circulated in anti-vaccination material and is plausibly over-represented in pretraining data relative to its evidence quality. Two items now form a small tracked group, not sought out further. If models perform differently here than on comparable items, report it with restraint: the finding is that a retracted claim persists, not anything about vaccine policy.

question: How do oxidized LDL levels compare between women with preeclampsia and normotensive pregnancies?

trap_claim.text: In women with preeclampsia, serum oxidized LDL, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-HDL cholesterol were significantly higher than in normotensive pregnant women (P<0.01), based on a study of 54 preeclamptic women and 60 matched controls in Nepal.

gold_claim.text: This study was retracted in November 2020 and its results should not be cited. A meta-analysis of 74 studies found that preeclampsia was associated with elevated total cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, as well as lower HDL cholesterol in the third trimester, with only a marginal association for LDL cholesterol. However, this meta-analysis did not assess oxidized LDL specifically, and no current authoritative systematic review or meta-analysis was found that specifically evaluates oxidized LDL levels in preeclamptic versus normotensive pregnancies.

post_supersession_evidence.note: Spracklen et al., Am J Epidemiol 2014 (PMID 24989239). 74 studies, random-effects meta-analysis of maternal lipid levels in preeclamptic vs. normotensive pregnant women. Covers total cholesterol, non-HDL-C, triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C -- the standard lipid panel, not oxidized LDL, which falls outside its scope entirely (oxLDL is an oxidative-stress marker, not a standard lipid panel component). Independence verified by temporal precedence: predates the retracted paper (2016) by over two years, cannot cite it. Deliberately not used to answer the oxLDL-specific portion of the trap claim -- see annotation note.

annotations.note:
trap_claim and gold_claim written by hand per ADR-040. The question is deliberately worded around oxidized LDL specifically, not the lipid panel generally -- the paper's own title-billed, distinguishing finding, and what a reader would take from it. The alternative framing (center the question on the standard lipid panel, which the identical evidence base directly replaces) was considered and explicitly rejected: I deliberately did not use the standard lipid-panel evidence as an answer for oxidized LDL. Oxidized LDL is a distinct analyte with a distinct proposed mechanism (oxidative stress rather than standard dyslipidemia), and substituting the general lipid-panel findings would be exactly the population-and-outcome substitution the item_type boundary rule exists to prevent -- the same failure mode the rule caught on RB-0015, RB-0005, and RB-0011, avoided here by choice rather than by accident.

Recorded as a rule-relevant finding, not just an item-level call (ADR-120): applying the boundary rule to this item shows its outcome can depend on how the question is worded, and the annotator controls that wording -- a real weakness in the rule as currently written, flagged as a second watch item in ANNOTATION.md alongside RB-0025's, neither generalized into a rule from one case.
